tagline: River-gravel pavement and brickwork connect three sites of colonial Virginia.
intro: The Colonial Parkway connects Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown across 23 miles between the James and York rivers. Broad curves, tree cover and river-view pull-offs shape the drive. Its unmarked pavement sets rounded river gravel into concrete, while brick-faced underpasses give the modern road a colonial-era appearance. The Federal Highway Administration lists it as an All-American Road and highlights both the historic sites and its parkway design.

National Park Service engineers and landscape architects surveyed the corridor in 1930. Between Yorktown and Williamsburg, planners chose a York River alignment across Navy land to avoid grade crossings and modern development. The Williamsburg tunnel was completed by 1942, but war, structural problems and flooding delayed traffic until 1949. During World War II, the Navy-land section closed to the public and served convoy training; in 1945, the Navy agreed to stop its transports and help restore the damaged landscape. The full route opened on April 27, 1957, in the year of Jamestown’s 350th anniversary.

Begin at Jamestown Island on the James River, then follow the corridor toward Williamsburg and its tunnel beneath the historic district. Beyond Williamsburg, the route crosses Navy land toward Yorktown on the York River. Pull-offs near both river ends offer broad views across the water, with historical markers explaining the scene.
notice: Rounded river gravel gives the concrete pavement an earth-toned surface.

moments.title: Historic Jamestowne
moments.text: The road’s approach to Jamestown Island is itself a reconstruction. Jamestown was a peninsula in colonial times; weather severed the connection, and parkway workers rebuilt the isthmus in the 1950s. River erosion also led visitors to believe that James Fort lay entirely underwater. Preservation Virginia funded a search led by William Kelso in 1994. By 1996, the team had found the fort, with only its western bulwark lost to erosion. The site includes ruins within the original 1607 fort and a church rebuilt in 1907 around its surviving seventeenth-century tower.

moments.title: Colonial Williamsburg
moments.text: The parkway’s tunnel carries the road beneath Colonial Williamsburg’s historic district. Finished by 1942, it did not carry traffic until 1949 because of war, structural problems and flooding. W. A. R. Goodwin and John D. Rockefeller Jr., with Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, were among the proponents of Williamsburg’s restoration in the late 1920s. Above it, the historic district combines restored buildings with later reconstructions. The Governor’s Palace and Capitol were reconstructed; the Courthouse, Magazine and Bruton Parish Church are original buildings. The road’s concealed passage was planned to reduce modern intrusions into this setting.

moments.title: Yorktown
moments.text: Yorktown began in 1691 as a York River port for exporting tobacco to Europe. In 1781, it became the site of the siege in which allied American and French forces defeated Cornwallis’s army. The battlefield retains many earthworks dug by the besieging forces. The town’s layout also keeps the river in view: Water Street follows the river beach, while Main Street occupies a bluff above the floodplain. Nine pre-Revolutionary buildings survive, including Nelson House and Somerwell House. The Yorktown Victory Monument commemorates the victory, the French alliance and the peace with Great Britain that followed the war.
